The recharge energy was compared with the baseline and HP-TES discharge energy to assess the grid impact during nighttime hours (Figure 39). Ideally, the recharge energy should be lower than the shifted energy to achieve energy savings, while cost savings rely on the peak and off-peak utility rates. Nonetheless, to ensure the grid is not strained at night, the energy required to recharge the TES should be below the baseline HP energy consumption during peak hours. It was found that the recharge energy was lower than the discharge energy during winter and shoulder seasons, suggesting that additional components and control improvements are required to minimize recharge energy demand, especially during the summer months, to (i) increase economic savings and (ii) achieve energy savings. However, the outdoor temperatures during TOU peak hours are close to the PCM melting temperature, with only 3 – 6 K difference. Thus, the demand reduction and the energy savings during the peak hours were between 6 – 22%, given the lower temperature lift decrease (Figure 41). The highest savings occurred in the summer months, as utility peak hours still had slightly higher outdoor temperatures than the rest of the year. Figure 41: Cumulative monthly energy consumption during the peak hours in Honolulu, HI Another option is to use the thermal battery during the thermodynamic peak and combine the HP-TES with an electric battery. This concept loads shifts at noontime to get maximum demand reduction and uses the saved energy to charge the electric battery. The peak energy savings ranged from 12% to 24% relative to the baseline. However, when the recharge energy was assessed, it was found to be around the baseline energy used during the peak. This is a challenge, as a more expensive electric battery will be required to recharge the HP-TES without using the electric grid.
